messages.subject: phylogram vs cladogram
messages.body_plain:
There have been a few papers that have discussed the utility in using phylograms instead of chronograms in ancestral character state analyses. A recent article (and citations for other studies within) is here <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13872>.

Because many biogeographic questions are intrinsically tied to timing it is logical to use a dated phylogeny for BioGeoBEARS.

I do not have the correct sampling to accurately date my current phylogeny. I am therefore wondering if anyone has looked into the utility of running BioGeoBEARS with a phylogeny where branch lengths correspond to molecular evolution instead of time?

The biggest issue I can think of is that logic of the linked paper does not necessarily extend into biogeography. That is, phenotypes are linked to molecular evolution hence the suitability of phylograms. But, biogeography may have a stronger link to time than to molecular evolution?

Any thoughts on this are appreciated. I have an idea where the center of origin is for my species is, but it would be ideal to have an analysis to test this theory.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Understanding how areas-allowed affects models with j parameter
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Understanding how areas-allowed affects models with j parameter
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Ivan, that all makes sense!

On Friday, April 29, 2022 at 10:23:31 AM UTC-4 ilf.ma...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Tom, from what you describe, it seems the model is running correctly. The "areas allowed" option will only affect anagenetic dispersal (modeled with the parameter d) in this case -- species cannot disperse from A to C forming the range AC. But cladogenetic dispersal (modeled with j) is always the dispersal from a previous range to a single new area, so A > C is allowed because it does not go through the prohibited range AC.
>
> You can probably disallow A > C by editing the distance matrix or manual dispersal multipliers, and setting dispersal between these areas to 0 -- but I am not sure if this affects both d and j, or only d.
>
> Hope this helps!
> Best,
> Ivan
>
> Em qua., 27 de abr. de 2022 às 10:38, Tom <tmor...@gmail.com> escreveu:
> >
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have been running the 'out of the box' approach, and had a question about how disallowing areas affects the j parameter (if it does). I am trying to constrain the biogeographic estimations to adjacent areas, and so constrained the state space, as found on the biogeobears tutorials. However, in the models that add in the j parameter, the areas are allowed to transition directly between non-adjacent areas.
> >
> > E.g.:
> > A <-> B <-> C = not allowing AC, but seeing a transition in my trees of A->C
> >
> > I understand that the founder-event speciation events could look like this, and that classic examples do exactly this. However, since I am studying aquatic organisms in adjacent freshwater systems, I want to ensure I am considering the implications (or unlikely nature) of passing directly through a system without range expansion. Presumably, if long-distance dispersal is allowed, the j-parameter should allow skipping several adjacent areas as well (if this scenario is most likely). If simulating adjacent areas is only intended for the models without the j parameter, then I believe the code is running correctly.
> >
> > Thank you,
> > Tom

messages.subject: Re: phylogram vs cladogram
messages.body_plain:
I was just reading this post http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#fix_short_trees and perhaps this advice from Dr. Matzke is the way to go, "If you have no good external dating information, but you want to estimate relative dates anyway (which is legitimate, if you state this clearly in your writeup), then in the BEAST setup, you should just put a tight normal prior on the date of the root, and give it a mean of, say, 1 or 10 or some such. Then you just recognize that all of your dates are relative to that prior constraint, and interpret your results accordingly."

I just haven't seen that in other papers. Anyone have experience with this?

I've run a few rounds of biogeobears with an undated tree and although the results are as expected in terms of center of origin I get otherwise wonky results.

messages.subject_clean: error: tip range not allowed in states_list
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to rerun BioGeoBEARS from a script I was using this past January (which ran successfully), but this time with more taxa in my tree and a new matrix in the areas_allowed file. I am not sure if a package updated (I did not update BioGeoBEARS or R), but now my script won't run. There seems to be an issue with the areas_allowed.txt file, but I cannot figure out what it is. I keep getting the following error:

Error in tipranges_to_tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state(tipranges, phy,  :
  STOP ERROR in tipranges_to_tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state():

Your geography file has a tip range which is not allowed in your specified state space (states_list).

The tip is: CR
The 0-based areas in the range is/are: '0_5'
The letter codes in the range are: 'I_S'

Try editing either the geography file, the areas_allowed or areas_adjacency matrices, or the states_list (non-stratified) / lists_of_states_lists_0based (stratified).

I am following the tutorial and this worked just a few months ago; I tried rerunning the script from January, which worked perfectly and I left it untouched, and now get the same error. Attached are the files I am trying to work with. All taxon names in my tree match those in my other files. Any ideas on what is causing this error and how to fix this?

Any help would be appreciated!
